authored_explainer.title: Cereal Production Is 1.5x Higher Than in 1972
authored_explainer.hook: The 1970s warned of food shortages. Cereal output did the opposite.
says: In 1985, progression to secondary school was 77.8; by 2017, 91.3—1.2 times higher, meaning access widened.
In 1972, cereal production was 1083.7 million metric tons; by 2024, 1644.1—1.5 times higher, meaning scarcity forecasts missed.
China leads with 5.2 million square kilometers of farmland; United States 4.2, Australia 3.6, Brazil 2.4, Russia 2.2—land alone isn't destiny.
authored_explainer.closing: More food came from productivity, not simply adding farmland.
authored_explainer.question: What changed food production most?

authored_explainer.title: Waste Energy Is 3.0x Higher Than in 1990
authored_explainer.hook: Since 1990, waste energy tripled—and methane rose with it.
says: In 1990, combustible renewables and waste supplied 10.2% of energy; by 2024, 30.1%—3.0 times higher, turning waste into fuel.
In 1998, access to electricity was 73.2%; by 2024, 91.9%—1.3 times higher, meaning more people gained power.
In 1972, methane emissions from waste were 903.8 Mt CO2e; by 2024, 1,652 Mt CO2e—1.8 times higher, despite energy recovery.
authored_explainer.closing: Using waste for energy still leaves an emissions problem to solve.
authored_explainer.question: Should waste energy count as clean?

authored_explainer.title: Population Growth Fell 54% Since 1972—But Population Rose
authored_explainer.hook: Population growth slowed sharply, but that never meant population decline.
says: In 1972, rural population was 63.1%; by 2025, 42.2%—down to 67% of that, showing the urban shift.
In 1972, population in the largest city was 18.2%; by 2025, 16.2%—barely moved, as growth spread elsewhere.
In 1972, population growth was 2%; by 2025, 0.91%—down to 46% of that, meaning slower growth, not decline.
authored_explainer.closing: Slower growth still adds people, so cities must plan without assuming decline.
authored_explainer.question: How should cities plan for slower growth?
